questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Units of a Derivative
questions.problem: A battery lasts $L(t)$ hours when it is charged for $t$ minutes. What are the units of $\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We have that the battery duration $L(t)$ is measured in hours and the charging time is measured in minutes. 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(t): & \text{hours} \\ t: & \text{minutes}\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative $\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}$ measures a change in $L(t)$ over a change in $t.$ So, it represents a ratio of the units:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}: & \frac{\text{hours}}{\text{minute}}\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, $\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}$ is measured in "hours per minute".

evidence.solution_quote: In other words, $\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}$ is measured in "hours per minute".

questions.problem: The decay rate $M$ of muons in a beam traveling at high speed can be modeled by the function $M(t)=2\cdot {e}^{-2t},$ where $t$ is the time, in microseconds, since observations started. What will be the decay rate of the muons after $0.5$ microseconds? Round your answer to three decimal places.

The function $M(t)$ models the decay rate for the particles $t$ microseconds since observations started.

Thus, the decay rate of the muons after $0.5$ microseconds is

$$
\begin{aligned}M(0.5) & =2\cdot {e}^{-2(0.5)} \\  & =2\cdot {e}^{-1} \\  & ≈0.736.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the decay rate of the particles is $0.736$ muons per microsecond.

questions.problem:
The birth rate of a herd of elephants in a region in Africa is modeled by the function  $B(t)=500\cdot {2}^{0.125t}$ while the rate of death is modeled by $D(t)=400\cdot {3}^{0.125t}.$ In both cases, $t$ represents the number of years since $1990.$

questions.worked_solution:
The  rate of change in the number of elephants  $t$ years since $1990$ is equal to the difference between the two given rates, that is

$$
\begin{aligned}B(8)-D(8) & =500\cdot {2}^{0.125(8)}-400\cdot {3}^{0.125(8)} \\  & =500\cdot 2-400\cdot 3 \\  & =-200.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change in the elephant population was $-200$ elephants per year.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change
questions.problem:
The rate $O$ of the orders a car factory receives can be modeled as $O(t)=100t{e}^{-0.1t}$ cars per day. The rate at which cars are completed can be modeled as $C(t)=50+10sin⁡(\frac{2\pi }{7}t)$ cars per day. In both cases, $t$ is the time, in days, since the launch of the new model. 

What is the rate of change in the number of cars under construction $28$ days after the model's launch? Assume that an ordered car goes into construction as soon as the factory receives its order. Round your answer to the nearest integer.
questions.worked_solution:
The rate of change of the number of cars under construction at time $t$ is equal to the order rate minus the completion rate, that is,

$$
O(t)-C(t).
$$

Substituting $t=28,$ the rate of change in the number of cars under construction after $28$ days is

$$
\begin{aligned}O(t)-C(t) & =100(28){e}^{-0.1(28)}-(50+10sin⁡(\frac{2\pi }{7}(28))) \\  & =100(28){e}^{-2.8}-50-10sin⁡(8\pi ) \\  & =100(28){e}^{-2.8}-50 \\  & ≈120.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change in the number of cars in construction after $28$ days is $120$ cars per day.

questions.problem:
Jason, a biologist, is measuring the growth of bacteria in a Petri dish by recording the following two numbers for different values of $t,$ where $t$ is the time, in hours, since he started his observations:

The function $N(t)$ gives the number of users $t$ days after the platform is set up. Then,

$$
{N}^{′}(t)=O(t)-C(t).
$$

Thus, ${N}^{′}(t)$ gives the rate at which the number of children inside the playground changes $t$ hours after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of children inside the playground at time $t$ by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time $t.$ That is,

$$
{N}^{′}(t)=E(t)-L(t).
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Units of a Derivative
canonical_examples.problem: A rocket is at a distance of $r(t)$ meters from the ground $t$ seconds after it is launched. What are the units of $\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}t}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We have that the height $r(t)$ is measured in meters and the time is measured in seconds. 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t): & \text{meters} \\ t: & \text{seconds}\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative $\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}t}$ measures a change in $r(t)$ over a change in $t.$ So, it represents a ratio of the units:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}: & \frac{\text{meters}}{\text{seconds}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}t}$ is measured in "meters per second".

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Interpreting the Derivative of a Function
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider a spherical balloon with radius $r.$ As the balloon loses air, its volume $V$ decreases. What is the best interpretation of $V'(r)?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13930198/assets/7f52288ca4670375413ecd5283bc2d15fbb332af311ead07986c1526d25e338a.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function $V(r)$ gives the volume of a sphere with radius $r.$ So

$$
V'(r) = \dfrac{\textrm{d}V}{\textrm{d}r} = \dfrac{\textrm{Change in }V}{\textrm{Change in }r}.
$$

Therefore, $V'(r)$ is the rate at which the volume changes as the radius changes.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Interpreting the Derivative of a Function in a Given Context
canonical_examples.problem: The function $B(s)$ models a school's budget, in dollars, given the average number of students $s$ in each grade. What is the best interpretation of $B'(30)=2\,000?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function $B'(s)$ represents the rate at which the budget is changing at the moment when the school has an average of exactly $s$ students in each grade.

Therefore, $B'(30) = 2\,000$ means:

*When the school has an average of $30$ students in each grade, its budget is increasing at a rate of $2\,000$ dollars per student.*

canonical_examples.problem:
On a particular day, the rate $E$ at which tourists enter a small country can be modeled as $E(t) = 50\cdot 3^{0.2t}$ tourists per hour, where $t$ is the time, in hours, after midnight. The rate at which tourists leave the country can be modeled as $L(t)=100\cdot 2^{0.2t}$ tourists per hour, where $t$ is also the time in hours after midnight.

What is the rate of change in the number of tourists in the country at $10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The rate of change of the number of tourists in the country at time $t$ is equal to the entry rate minus the exit rate at time $t,$ that is, 

$$
E(t)-L(t).
$$

Since $10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}$ is ten hours after midnight, we have $t=10.$ Substituting $t=10,$ the rate of change in the number of tourists in the country at $10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}E(10)-L(10) & =50\cdot {3}^{0.2(10)}-100\cdot {2}^{0.2(10)} \\  & =450-400 \\  & =50.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change in the number of tourists in the country at $10\text{:}00\,\textrm{am}$ is $50$ tourists per hour.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Relating a Derivative to a Rate of Change
canonical_examples.problem:
Howard, the manager of a sci-fi convention, uses the following three functions to model the daily number of visitors to the convention, $t$ minutes after the convention has opened.

- $N(t)$ - the number of people inside the convention

- $E(t)$ - the rate at which people enter the convention

- $L(t)$ - the rate at which people leave the convention

What is the relationship between the three functions above?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function $N(t)$ gives the number of people inside the convention $t$ minutes after opening. Then,

$$
N'(t) = \dfrac{\textrm{d}N(t)}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{\textrm{Change in }N}{\textrm{Change in }t}.
$$

Thus, $N'(t)$ gives the rate at which the number of people inside the convention changes $t$ minutes after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of people inside the convention at time $t$ by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time $t.$ That is,

$$
N'(t) = E(t) - L(t).
$$
